did_you_know.text: The chapter opens with the repeated statement, “There was no king in Israel.” The Levite lived in the remote hill country of Ephraim, and his concubine was from Bethlehem in Judah.
The concubine left the Levite and returned to her father’s house in Bethlehem in Judah, where she stayed for four months.
The Levite went after his concubine to “speak tenderly to her” and bring her back. He took his servant and a pair of donkeys with him.
The woman’s father welcomed the Levite gladly, hosted him in his home, and for three days they ate, drank, and spent the nights there.
On the fifth day, the woman’s father continued urging the Levite to eat and stay longer, until the day was nearly over. Thus, his hospitality once again delayed their departure.

The Levite refused to spend the night in Jebus, that is, Jerusalem, because he regarded it as a foreign city. He preferred to continue to an Israelite settlement and eventually reached Gibeah in the territory of Benjamin.

When they arrived in Gibeah, the Levite sat in the city square, but no one took them into his home. Only an old man from the hill country of Ephraim, who lived in Gibeah, came and offered them hospitality.
The men of the city are described as “worthless men.” They surrounded the house and demanded that the guest be brought out to them so they could sexually abuse him.
After the night’s abuse, the woman returned to the entrance of the house at daybreak and collapsed there. When the Levite opened the door, he found her with her hands on the threshold.

The Levite cut his concubine’s body into twelve pieces and sent them throughout the territory of Israel. The act was intended to shock all the tribes and move them to discuss the tragedy and how to respond to it.

The people’s response emphasizes the gravity of the event: they said that nothing like it had been seen since the Israelites came up from the land of Egypt, and they urged everyone who saw it to consult together and speak.
